```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

RESULTS = Path("../../experiments/003-affine-augmentation/results")
runs = pd.read_csv(RESULTS / "runs.csv")
history = pd.read_csv(RESULTS / "history.csv")
for frame in (runs, history):
    frame["clean"] = frame["clean_accuracy"] * 100
    frame["perturbed"] = frame["shifted_accuracy"] * 100
runs["gap"] = runs["clean"] - runs["perturbed"]

ARMS = {"none": "No augmentation", "affine": "Affine augmentation"}
# Categorical slots 1 and 2 of the palette, checked for colour-vision separation on this surface.
COLOR = {"none": "#2a78d6", "affine": "#eb6834"}
SURFACE, INK, MUTED, GRID = "#fcfcfb", "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#e4e3df"

plt.rcParams.update(
    {
        "figure.facecolor": SURFACE,
        "axes.facecolor": SURFACE,
        "savefig.facecolor": SURFACE,
        "axes.edgecolor": GRID,
        "axes.labelcolor": MUTED,
        "axes.titlecolor": INK,
        "axes.titlesize": 10,
        "axes.titleweight": "bold",
        "axes.titlelocation": "left",
        "axes.spines.top": False,
        "axes.spines.right": False,
        "axes.spines.left": False,
        "axes.grid": True,
        "axes.grid.axis": "y",
        "grid.color": GRID,
        "grid.linewidth": 0.8,
        "xtick.color": MUTED,
        "ytick.color": MUTED,
        "xtick.bottom": False,
        "ytick.left": False,
        "font.size": 9,
        "legend.frameon": False,
    }
)

stats = runs.groupby("arm")[["clean", "perturbed", "gap"]].agg(["mean", "std"])


def cell(arm, column):
    return f"{stats.loc[arm, (column, 'mean')]:.2f} ± {stats.loc[arm, (column, 'std')]:.2f}"


def mean(arm, column):
    return stats.loc[arm, (column, "mean")]


gain = mean("affine", "perturbed") - mean("none", "perturbed")
cost = mean("none", "clean") - mean("affine", "clean")
largest_spread = max(stats.loc["none", ("perturbed", "std")], stats.loc["affine", ("perturbed", "std")])
gaps = ", ".join(f"{value:.2f}" for value in runs.loc[runs["arm"] == "affine", "gap"])
first = history[history["epoch"] == history["epoch"].min()].groupby("arm")[["clean", "perturbed"]].mean()
last = history[history["epoch"] == history["epoch"].max()].groupby("arm")[["clean", "perturbed"]].mean()
commit = runs["commit"].iloc[0][:7]
```

## Summary

A small convolutional network trained on MNIST loses about `{python} f"{mean('none', 'gap'):.0f}"` percentage
points of accuracy when the test digits are rotated, shifted and rescaled. Training with the same kind of
perturbation as augmentation recovers all but `{python} f"{mean('affine', 'gap'):.2f}"` points of that, at a cost
on unperturbed digits (`{python} f"{cost:.2f}"` points) that is no larger than the variation between random seeds.
The question asked whether augmentation closes the gap; by the threshold fixed before the experiment, one point, it
does not quite.

## Question

Does random affine augmentation during training close the accuracy gap between clean MNIST test digits and
affine-perturbed ones for a small CNN, and what does it cost on the clean digits?

Before any run, three outcomes were defined. The gap counts as closed if the augmented model's accuracy on perturbed
digits is within one point of its own accuracy on clean digits. Augmentation counts as helping without closing the
gap if accuracy on perturbed digits improves by more than twice the larger seed standard deviation while more than
one point remains. Anything else counts as no.

## Setup

The model has 105,866 parameters: two convolution blocks and one hidden layer. It was trained for
`{python} int(runs["epochs"].iloc[0])` epochs on the 60,000 MNIST training digits, in two arms that differ only in
the training transform, with three seeds per arm. One arm sees the digits as they are. The other sees every digit
under a fresh random rotation within ±20°, translation within ±3 pixels and scale between 0.85 and 1.15.

Both arms are evaluated on the 10,000 MNIST test digits and on a perturbed copy of them, in which each digit received
one random draw from the same ranges. The perturbed set is fixed and stored apart from the code, in the place a
private dataset would occupy. Because the test perturbation and the augmentation share their ranges, the experiment
measures the most favourable case for augmentation: the shift is known in advance.

## Results

```{python}
#| label: fig-accuracy
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy after the last epoch. Each dot is one seed; the bar marks the mean of three."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of accuracy on the clean and the perturbed test set for both arms. On clean digits all six models sit near 98.5 to 99 percent. On perturbed digits the unaugmented models sit near 83 to 85 percent and the augmented ones near 97.5 percent."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
positions = {"clean": 0, "perturbed": 1}
offsets = {"none": -0.2, "affine": 0.2}
for arm, label in ARMS.items():
    rows = runs[runs["arm"] == arm]
    for column, x in positions.items():
        center = x + offsets[arm]
        ax.scatter(
            [center] * len(rows), rows[column], s=46, color=COLOR[arm], edgecolor=SURFACE, linewidth=1.5, zorder=3,
            label=label if column == "clean" else None,
        )
        ax.hlines(rows[column].mean(), center - 0.09, center + 0.09, color=COLOR[arm], linewidth=2, zorder=2)
        # The mean's value sits on the outer side of each group, clear of the neighbouring arm.
        side = -1 if arm == "none" else 1
        ax.annotate(
            f"{rows[column].mean():.1f}",
            (center + side * 0.12, rows[column].mean()),
            va="center",
            ha="right" if side < 0 else "left",
            color=INK,
            fontsize=8.5,
        )
ax.set_xticks(list(positions.values()), ["Clean test digits", "Perturbed test digits"])
ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 1.6)
ax.set_ylim(80, 100)
ax.set_ylabel("Accuracy (%)")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", handletextpad=0.2)
plt.show()
```

| Arm | Clean test digits | Perturbed test digits | Gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No augmentation | `{python} cell("none", "clean")` | `{python} cell("none", "perturbed")` | `{python} cell("none", "gap")` |
| Affine augmentation | `{python} cell("affine", "clean")` | `{python} cell("affine", "perturbed")` | `{python} cell("affine", "gap")` |

: Accuracy in percent after the last epoch, mean ± standard deviation over three seeds. {#tbl-accuracy}

Augmentation raises accuracy on perturbed digits by `{python} f"{gain:.2f}"` points. The larger of the two seed
standard deviations is `{python} f"{largest_spread:.2f}"` points, so the improvement is far outside the noise. The
augmented model still scores `{python} f"{mean('affine', 'gap'):.2f}"` points lower on perturbed digits than on clean
ones, which is more than the one point that would have counted as closing the gap. The outcome is therefore the
middle one: augmentation helps but does not close the gap.

On clean digits the augmented arm is `{python} f"{cost:.2f}"` points lower. With three seeds and standard deviations
of `{python} f"{stats.loc['none', ('clean', 'std')]:.2f}"` and
`{python} f"{stats.loc['affine', ('clean', 'std')]:.2f}"` points, this experiment cannot tell that difference from
zero.

```{python}
#| label: fig-epochs
#| fig-cap: "Mean accuracy over three seeds after each epoch. Both panels share the vertical axis."
#| fig-alt: "Two line charts of accuracy by epoch. On clean digits both arms rise from about 98 to about 99 percent. On perturbed digits the unaugmented arm rises from 78 to 84 percent and is still rising, while the augmented arm rises from 94 to 97.5 percent and flattens."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.2), sharey=True)
per_epoch = history.groupby(["arm", "epoch"])[["clean", "perturbed"]].mean().reset_index()
for ax, column, title in zip(axes, ("clean", "perturbed"), ("Clean test digits", "Perturbed test digits")):
    for arm, label in ARMS.items():
        rows = per_epoch[per_epoch["arm"] == arm]
        ax.plot(rows["epoch"], rows[column], color=COLOR[arm], linewidth=2, solid_capstyle="round", label=label)
        ax.scatter(
            rows["epoch"].iloc[-1:], rows[column].iloc[-1:], s=46, color=COLOR[arm], edgecolor=SURFACE,
            linewidth=1.5, zorder=3,
        )
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
    ax.set_xticks(sorted(history["epoch"].unique()))
axes[0].set_ylabel("Accuracy (%)")
axes[0].set_ylim(75, 100)
axes[1].legend(loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## What else the runs showed

Two observations were not part of the question. Both have been filed as new questions and neither was tested here.

**The remaining gap may be digits that cannot be recovered.** For the three augmented models it is `{python} gaps`
points, with a standard deviation of `{python} f"{stats.loc['affine', ('gap', 'std')]:.2f}"`, while their clean and
perturbed accuracies each vary by more
(`{python} f"{stats.loc['affine', ('clean', 'std')]:.2f}"` and
`{python} f"{stats.loc['affine', ('perturbed', 'std')]:.2f}"`). The two accuracies move together, which is what one
would see if the models failed on much the same perturbed digits, for instance digits whose strokes the perturbation
pushed out of the frame. An earlier run of the same sweep showed this far more sharply, with gaps of 1.13, 1.09 and
1.17 points; the present run does not, and three seeds cannot settle it.

**The unaugmented model had not finished improving on perturbed digits.** Its accuracy there rose from
`{python} f"{first.loc['none', 'perturbed']:.1f}"`% after the first epoch to
`{python} f"{last.loc['none', 'perturbed']:.1f}"`% after the last, while its clean accuracy moved by
`{python} f"{last.loc['none', 'clean'] - first.loc['none', 'clean']:.1f}"` points (@fig-epochs). The gap reported
for the unaugmented arm is therefore an upper estimate of what a fully trained model would show.

A third observation concerns method. Accuracy on perturbed digits varied between seeds by
`{python} f"{stats.loc['none', ('perturbed', 'std')]:.2f}"` points for the unaugmented arm, against
`{python} f"{stats.loc['none', ('clean', 'std')]:.2f}"` points on clean digits. Three seeds were enough for an effect
of thirteen points. They would not be enough for an effect of half a point.

## Limits

The result holds for one model size, a short training schedule and three seeds per arm. The sweep was run twice with
the same seeds, under two software environments; single models differed by up to 0.18 points between the runs and
every mean agreed to within 0.1. The test perturbation was
drawn from the ranges used for augmentation; a shift the augmentation did not anticipate was not tested.
